item.research_question: What is the role of vibrational contributions in the thermodynamic stability of high-entropy carbides, and under what conditions should they be included in stability predictions?
item.material_system: (HfNbTaTiV)C, (HfNbTaTiW)C, and (HfNbTaTiZr)C (referred to as HEC-V, HEC-W, and HEC-Zr)
item.processing_route: Computational integration of the Partial Occupation (POCC) algorithm with the AFLOW Automatic Phonon Library (APL); structures relaxed until forces were below 10−3 eV/ℓ; phonon calculations used a displacement magnitude of 0.015 ℓ in supercells with at least 180 atoms; TPOCC set to 2473 K.
item.test_conditions: Harmonic approximation at temperatures ranging from 0 K to synthesis temperatures; comparison against binary carbide precursors (rock-salt phases) and decomposition products; Debye-Grüneisen model (AGL) used for comparison.
key_findings: Vibrational contributions shift the transition temperature for HEC-W by approximately 150 K, whereas they have only a small effect on HEC-V and HEC-Zr.
Mass disorder on the cation sublattice destabilizes the high-entropy carbides (increases vibrational free energy), while force constant disorder has a stabilizing effect.
The vibrational entropy change (ΔSvib) for HEC-W is 0.22 kB/atom, which is an order of magnitude larger than the 0.04 kB/atom observed for HEC-V and HEC-Zr.
The Debye-Grüneisen model (AGL) incorrectly predicts HEC-V to be more strongly stabilized by vibrations than HEC-W, failing to capture phonon anomalies present in VC.
Vibrational contributions shift the decomposition phase transition temperatures for HEC-V and HEC-W to lower temperatures by 80 K and 160 K, respectively.

The carbide sublattice distorts to accommodate different metal cations, resulting in nearest-neighbor metal-carbon distances that are closer to the average of binary carbides to maximize configurational entropy.
Vibrations alone are insufficient to stabilize HEC-V against decomposition at 2000 K, as the vibrational free energy change is smaller than the distance to the convex hull.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that vibrational contributions are significant when precursors or decomposition products have different nearest-neighbor environments or symmetries compared to the high-entropy carbide. Specifically, the lower symmetry of hexagonal WC compared to the rock-salt HEC-W leads to depressed vibrational entropy in the precursor, creating a large stabilization gain upon forming the disordered phase. Conversely, when precursors and the HEC share similar atomic environments (as in HEC-V and HEC-Zr), the vibrational entropy changes are minimal.
item.limitations: The study relies on the harmonic approximation, ignoring anharmonic effects which become significant at high temperatures and could stabilize structures with imaginary frequencies; the calculations use the PBE functional which may affect phonon frequencies; the ideal high-temperature configurational entropy is used, which overestimates entropic contributions at lower temperatures; and the study is limited to stoichiometric samples without accounting for vacancies or interstitial carbon.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that anharmonic contributions should be included to improve accuracy, that the effect of the exchange-correlation functional (e.g., SCAN vs. PBE) on transition temperatures needs investigation, and that defects such as vacancies and interstitial carbon atoms should be explored in future research on high-entropy ceramics.
quotes: The contribution of vibrations to the stability of high-entropy ceramics is still controversial.

Vibrational contributions have a measurable effect: even though the configurational entropy provides the predominant contribution to the formation of HEC-W, the vibrational contributions shift the transition temperature by approximately 150 K.
Vibrational contributions should be taken into account when one or more of the precursors or decomposition products have different nearest-neighbor environments from the high-entropy carbide.

item.research_question: How to generate and validate derivative structures for (HfNbTaTi)RC high-entropy carbides to ensure converged vibrational free energy calculations.
item.processing_route: Created 49 ordered representative structures using the AFLOW-POCC algorithm from a rock-salt parent structure (space group: Fm-3m, #225); KPPRA value increased until vibrational free energy at 300 K converged within 1 meV/atom; APL supercells generated using standard conventional representations; relaxation and static calculations performed with exact same k-point densities.
item.test_conditions: Vibrational free energy convergence target of 1 meV/atom at 300 K; k-point densities required to be identical for relaxation and static calculations to avoid residual force increases.
key_findings: 49 ordered representative structures were created for the (HfNbTaTi)RC system.
KPPRA values were increased until vibrational free energy at 300 K was converged within 1 meV/atom.
Using different k-point densities for relaxation and static calculations leads to an increase in residual forces by up to two orders of magnitude.
This residual force increase was observed even at KPPRA values above 20,000.
Standard conventional representations were used to generate APL supercells to achieve a more spherical shape.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that maintaining exact same k-point densities for relaxation and static calculations is critical to prevent large residual forces, which can occur even at high KPPRA values if densities differ.
quotes: vibrational free energy at 300 K was converged within 1 meV/atom.
Doing otherwise leads to an increase in residual forces by up to two orders of magnitude.
